newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers back line-item vetoes on tax bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers back line-item vetoes on tax bill.

text.p: Two U.S. House of Representatives leaders said Sunday they would support President Clinton if he used line-item vetoes to remove "outrageous" provisions from a mammoth tax bill.
House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri said on NBC-TV's "Meet the Press" that a tobacco industry provision deserved excission -- "It's a bad provision. It ought to come out."
House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, Ohio Republican, also interviewed on NBC, said he would support use of the line-item veto but did not name a target.
"If there are provisions in there...that are clearly outrageous, I would support the president doing it," he said.
A House-Senate committee identified 80 provisions in the tax bill, worked out in negotiations with the White House and passed by Congress last week, that could be vulnerable to line-item veto.

The line-item veto law, which took effect at the start of this year, allows veto of a "limited tax benefit" that affects 100 or fewer taxpayers. The Supreme Court rejected in June a challenge to the law. Clinton has not employed the law.

As part of the tax bill, Congress voted that money raised from a 15-cent increase in the tax on a pack of cigarettes would be counted toward the $368 billion the industry would pay in a proposed settlement of state and class-action lawsuits.
The per-pack federal tax now is 24 cents.

On Friday a White House spokesman said the tobacco provision might not be subject to the line-item veto law. Administration officials said any settlement with the tobacco industry may need to be increased to offset the tax-bill provision.
